feedback.worked_solution:
As $x$ approaches $1$ from the left, the function $g(x)$ approaches $1.$ Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{-}}g(x)=1.
$$

Likewise, as $x$ approaches $1$ from the right, the function $g(x)$ approaches $0.$ Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{+}}g(x)=0.
$$

In conclusion, we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{-}}g(x)=1,\,{lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{+}}g(x)=0.
$$

In part 1, we showed that

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{-}}g(x)=1,\,{lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{+}}g(x)=0.
$$

Since ${lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{-}}g(x)\ne {lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{+}}g(x),$ we conclude that

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,1}g(x)=\text{DNE}.
$$

From the graph, we see that as we approach $x=-1$ from the left, the $y$-value approaches $1.$ So the left-hand limit is

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,(-1)^{-}}g(x)=1.
$$

Similarly, when we approach $x=-1$ from the right, the $y$-value again approaches $1.$ So the right-hand limit is

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,(-1)^{+}}g(x)=1.
$$

Since both the left and right-hand limits exist and are equal to $1,$ we conclude that

 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,(-1)}g(x)=1.
$$

earlier_parts.problem:

                                        ${lim}_{x\to \infty }g(x)=$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-2}}

feedback.worked_solution:
On the left side of the graph, we see that as the values of $x$ decrease and approach $-\infty ,$ the graph of the function $g(x)$ moves closer and closer to the horizontal asymptote $y=-1.$

Consequently, $g(x)$ approaches the value $-1$ as $x$ approaches $-\infty ,$ and we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to -\infty }g(x)=-1.
$$

On the right side of the graph, as the values of $x$ increase and approach $\infty ,$  the graph of the function $g(x)$ moves closer and closer to the horizontal asymptote $y=-1.$ Therefore, 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }g(x)=-1.
$$
